items.title: Show HN: RayClay – an open source C app framework for desktop, mobile, and web
items.summary: RayClay aims to be the most developer-friendly framework for creating native desktop and mobile applications. It handles all the DIY aspects of C for you while retaining all the performance benefits of using a low-level programming language. MY MOTIVATION At the start of the year I decided I wanted to develop my own app with the goal of releasing it on mobile, desktop, and web. Probably like most developers, I wanted to build a closed-source app and distribute it to whomever I wanted. And I didn't want to have to pay any sort of fee or owe any conditions to the development tools I used. It turns out, this set of criteria really limited what framework I could choose. Distributing it to whomever I wanted meant that the app had to be properly cross-platform. This cut out options like React Native (no official Linux) and Electron (no iOS or Android). And, while Tauri has yeses for all platforms, I decided that its dependence on platform-native webviews would probably mean excessive ongoing maintenance which I would prefer not to have to deal with. These frameworks were all very bloated anyways so it didn't feel like a big loss tbh. So I was left with choosing between Qt and Flutter, but Qt has this finicky dual licensing model and Flutter still felt a bit too bloated. Ultimately, I realised that I was looking for a framework that didn't exist: lightweight like Qt but also convenient and fully open-source like Flutter. I wanted the performance of a lower-level framework with the convenience of less-performant frameworks. Is that really so much to ask for :/ This led me to develop RayClay. It's already 6 months old but now I feel it is really ready for the world to check it out since I've released v1.0 (which I deliberately held back releasing until I though it was ready). This description is adapted from my blog post here https://www.impizulu.com/blog/why-i-built-rayclay where I give a little more detail.

items.title: Show HN: Relaticle, an open-source CRM that Claude and ChatGPT can work in
items.summary: I asked rela (the assistant inside my open source crm relaticle) once for a task and a note (in a test workspace). It shows me a plan, one line per change, one approve button. There was no task or note until I clicked approve. Relaticle (my open source CRM) has an MCP server for AI agents right in the core app. Claude and ChatGPT connect to it, and over the MCP protocol, they don't need a plan, they don't need an approve button, the writes just land right away. Not sure yet if those writes should wait for approval too. I started writing this in August 2024. It's written in Laravel + PostgreSQL. I'm releasing it under the AGPL-3.0 license. If you want to try it out you can run it using the compose file in the README. I'm very interested in hearing from people who let an agent write to a real system and what they have to say about it.

Show HN: Rmux – A lightweight GPU rendered terminal workspace
items.summary: Hey HN, I've been working on rmux, an open source terminal workspace built in Rust using GPUI and Ghostty's terminal engine. The main focus has been performance. I wanted something that could handle multiple projects, shells and coding agents without becoming a resource hog or feeling sluggish as more panes are opened, which has been a frustration I've had with some other terminals. I also have a sweet setup for it to be my standard external terminal for VS Code where I can switch back and forth between the same workspace in VS Code and rmux with a single shortcut. I share the details of how that's done on the VS Code page on the website. It supports named workspaces, tabs, split panes, keyboard shortcuts and a command palette. Nothing particularly revolutionary in terms of features, but the goal is to make the experience as responsive and lightweight as possible. Of course the site has a WASM demo - because it's in Rust and that's what the cool people do. Would be interested to hear what people think, particularly around performance and the overall UX. Source is on GitHub, linked from the website.
